suom1saundi – Manual

suom1saundi is firmware for the M-VAVE FM-1 that turns the little FM synth into a groovebox for suomisaundi: Finnish freestyle psytrance. The genre is bouncy, playful and silly, with rolling basses, chirping acid lines, chiptune melodies and noises nobody expects. The six voices are built for exactly that, and a knob called SEKO (Finnish for "crazy") makes sure no bar sounds quite like the last.

There are two ways to play it: MINI, the FM-1 alone, and MAXI, the FM-1 with an M-VAVE SMK-37 (Pro or Elite) as its control centre, with keys, 16 pads, 8 endless knobs and faders.

This manual updates itself: the tables of knobs, factory values, pages, scales, the SMK-37 map and versions are written by tools/manual.py straight from the firmware's code on every push.

Status and warning

  • The core (app/core/suomi.c) runs in the host tests, in fm1-base's simulator and in the browser emulator.
  • A .fwsc package for the device needs JieLi's toolchain and the AC79 SDK and has not been built yet.
  • The firmware has not been tested on a real FM-1, nor with a real SMK-37. Custom firmware can brick a device. Go to the official V15 first, back up your data and know how to get back (fm1-base's installer).
  • Projects saved by version 0.1 are not loaded (the format changed); the FM-1 then starts with a fresh groove.

Try it without the device

The emulator runs in the browser with exactly the same C core as the firmware, as WebAssembly. The controls sit as on the FM-1. Press Ton einschalten (sound on) first, then PLAY. The space bar is PLAY. Saving goes to the browser.

Below the FM-1 sits a virtual SMK-37 with knobs, faders, pads, a mod wheel and two octaves of keys (also A W S E D F T G Y H U J K on the computer). It sends the factory map. A real SMK-37 (or any controller) on the computer plays the emulator through Web MIDI (Chrome or Edge).

Quick start

  1. Press PLAY: a generated groove in F♯ phrygian dominant at 145 BPM plays out of the box.
  2. One of the first six black keys picks a track. The 16 white keys are its steps.
  3. SEL rolls the track anew, ARP changes it just a little, the black key NEW rolls the whole groove with a new chord, UNDO brings the previous one back.
  4. HOME and turn up KNOB3 (SEKO): the groove starts to improvise.
  5. EDIT and turn the four knobs: the track's sound. EDIT again: the other four sound knobs. A third time: the track's LFO.
  6. ENV: the mixer with all six tracks.
  7. A short press on SAVE stores everything.

MOD: each track's LFO

EDIT ×3 opens the chosen track's LFO. It runs in time with the groove and moves one sound knob, hit by hit: an acid line whose filter opens over two bars, a kick that hits harder every other bar, zaps that fray further and further.

  • RATE: one cycle per 1/16, 1/8, 3/16, 1/4, 3/8, 1/2, 3/4, 1, 2 or 4 bars
  • SHAPE: SIN, TRI, SAW (falling), SQR, RND (a new random value each cycle)
  • DEST: which of the eight sound knobs
  • DEPTH: 0 in the middle; right for more, left inverted

The generator

SEL (one track) and NEW (the whole groove) don't just place hits, they write note lines that fit together:

  • Each pattern has a chord (GLO ×2, CHORD: a degree of the scale, I to VII). BASSO, HAPPO, PIIP and OUTO build their notes from that chord and the scale, so they agree.
  • BASSO gallops on the chord's root, jumps to the octave, the fifth and sometimes the note below; one line in three ends on the fifth.
  • HAPPO plays a motif of eight notes over a rhythm cell: pedal notes with jumps, broken chords, runs through the scale, the phrygian squeak. The second time round its second half sometimes moves up a third. Big jumps slide, octave jumps get accents.
  • PIIP plays question and answer: eight notes that come home to the root. Where HAPPO plays, PIIP often leaves a gap, so the two answer each other.
  • OUTO throws its zaps onto chord tones, an octave up or down.
  • From the factory, patterns A to D are a chord progression (such as I – VI – VII – I). With CHAIN (GLO) the groove walks through it. NEW picks a new chord for the pattern.
  • ARP (mutate) also puts the notes it changes on chord tones.

The sequencer

  • Polymetre: each track has its own loop length (ALGORITHM). HAPPO on 14 against the kick's 16 repeats only after seven bars.
  • Chance per step, ratchets of up to four hits, accents.
  • Slides on BASSO, HAPPO and PIIP: the sound glides to the new note without a new attack. The glide time is GLIDE (fixed on PIIP). A slide is only heard while the previous note still sounds.
  • Parameter locks: on EDIT, hold a white key and turn K1 to K4: the value holds for that step alone. The generator gives OUTO its own locks on every step, which is why each zap sounds different.
  • EUCLID (SEQ): hits spread as evenly as the loop allows, with rotation, chance and an accent on every n-th hit.
  • LINK (SEQ ×2): the track plays depending on another: WITH only when the source hits, GAPS only in its gaps, AFTER a step later. A muted source still counts.
  • TIMING (SEQ ×3): SELECT walks from hit to hit, K1 shifts the hit, K2 the whole track.

SEKO

SEKO on the HOME page is the suomisaundi knob. At 0 the sequencer plays exactly what is programmed. The further up, the more often a step plays something else: a scale degree up or down, an octave off, with a slide or as a double hit; hats double or swap their accent. Filters and decays wander slowly too, and the level sways a little. The kick always stays where it is. In MAXI, SEKO sits on the SMK-37's mod wheel.

The mixer

ENV opens the mixer. Instead of the steps the screen then shows all six tracks as channel strips: a level meter, the fader, the delay and reverb sends, the pan, M for muted and S for solo. The knobs work on the chosen track (pick it as ever: black keys, SELECT, OCT).

  • MIX (ENV): LEVEL, PAN, DELAY, REVERB.
  • CHANNEL (ENV ×2): TONE, a gentle filter per channel (FLAT in the middle, left a low-pass, right a high-pass), BITS and RATE (the 8-bit crusher) and DUCK, how far the track gives way to the kick. The strips show LP, HP and 8.
  • MASTER (ENV ×3): DRIVE saturates the sum, D.RET and R.RET are the delay's and reverb's returns, WIDTH the stereo width (0 mono, 64 as is, 127 wide). At the right edge the screen shows the sum, left and right.
  • FX and FX ×2 set the delay, the reverb and the sidechain.
  • In MAXI the SMK-37's faders are the mixer: F1 to F6 the tracks' levels, F7 and F8 the delay's and reverb's returns.

8-bit

ENV twice opens the chosen track's CHANNEL page:

  • BITS rounds the signal to fewer and fewer levels (OFF, then coarser up to 127).
  • RATE holds each value for several samples: the sample rate drops, the sound turns metallic and full of aliasing.

On top of that, PIIP (pulse waves, 4-bit triangle, pitched noise) and HATTU's CHIP knob (a shift register like a sound chip's) already sound 8-bit by themselves. The idea comes from memetek-fm1.

Effects and sidechain

  • FX: delay time (1/16, 1/8, 3/16; the right side two thirds of it), feedback, reverb size, damping.
  • FX ×2 (SIDECHAIN): source (POTKU from the factory), depth, release and how much the chosen track is ducked. A muted source still ducks (ghost kick).

MINI and MAXI

MINI is the FM-1 alone: everything goes through its 4 knobs, pages and keys, as above.

MAXI is the FM-1 with an M-VAVE SMK-37 (Pro or Elite). The SMK-37 becomes the control centre: its keys play the chosen track, the pads play the drums and switch tracks, the 8 knobs (16 with KNOB BANK) sit on the sound knobs, the faders are the mixer. As soon as the FM-1 gets a message from the SMK-37 it switches to MAXI: a green line appears under the logo, and on the EDIT and EDIT² pages the screen shows all eight sound knobs at once; the one last turned on the SMK-37 is lit.

Connecting

  • Cable (recommended): the SMK-37's 3.5 mm MIDI out into the FM-1's MIDI jack (with the right adapters). The firmware needs no extra code for it.
  • Through a computer: SMK-37 and FM-1 on the computer by USB, MIDI routed from the SMK-37 to the FM-1.
  • Bluetooth is left out on purpose: a Bluetooth stack takes a large part of the FM-1's flash and RAM.

The map

From the factory the FM-1 expects the map below. The easiest way is to set the SMK-37 the same in MIDI SUITE (M-VAVE's editor). Or the FM-1 learns the map the SMK-37 sends now:

  1. Press GLO three times: the SMK-37 page.
  2. SEL: the screen guides you. Play a key (the C that should be the base note), hit pad 1, switch PAD BANK on and hit pad 17, then turn K1 to K16 one after the other, move F1 to F8 and press ◀ and ▶ last (for K9 to K16 press KNOB BANK first, for F5 to F8 FADER BANK).
  3. SEL skips a control, SAVE ends the learning (the rest stays unassigned), HOME cancels.

Endless knobs that send steps instead of positions are recognised while learning. ARP on the SMK-37 page brings back the factory map. K1 on that page turns MAXI off; K2 to K4 set the channels of keys, pads and knobs by hand.

K1 to K4 write parameter locks while a white key is held on the FM-1. Pads 1 to 6 sound at once, with velocity; with REC and the groove running they are written, like the keys, into the step they fall on.

The six buttons under the display

  • KNOB BANK switches the knobs to K9 to K16 (LFO and channel), FADER BANK the faders to F5 to F8.
  • PAD BANK: press KNOB BANK and FADER BANK together. The pads become pads 17 to 32, and on the FM-1 those are the chosen track's 16 steps: a hit switches a step on or off, a hard hit sets it with an accent. A step past the loop's end makes the loop that long. So you program from the SMK-37 as on a drum machine: pick the track with pads 1 to 6 (PAD BANK off), set its steps with PAD BANK.
  • ◀ and ▶ switch the pattern (A to D), while playing at the next bar. Set them to CC 102 and 103 in MIDI SUITE, or let the FM-1 learn them.
  • OCTAVE− and OCTAVE+ move the keys by octaves. The SMK-37 does that itself; the FM-1 simply gets higher or lower notes, on the chosen track and when recording with REC.

In the emulator the virtual SMK-37 has the same six buttons under a small display showing the banks and the octave. With a mouse, shift-click on a BANK button toggles PAD BANK.

What the SMK-37 takes over

The SMK-37 has its own arpeggiator, chord mode, scale correction and note repeat. suom1saundi does not build them again: what the SMK-37 plays with them arrives as notes, sounds on the chosen track and is recorded with REC.

Patterns, chain and key

Four patterns, A to D. PRESETS switches them, while playing at the next bar. CHAIN (GLO) plays A-B, A-C or A-D in turn, four bars each. Each pattern has its chord (GLO ×2, CHORD) and can be transposed with XPOSE. Hold SAVE and turn PRESETS to copy the whole pattern, hold SAVE and turn SELECT to copy the track alone; letting go copies, UNDO in the destination takes it back.

MIDI

  • In (TRS jack and USB): with MAXI on, notes on the keys' channel (1 from the factory) play the chosen track and the pad notes (channel 10, 36 to 51 from the factory) are the pads; CCs and pitch bend as in the map above. Without MAXI and on the other channels: channels 1 to 6 play the tracks (note 60 = the step's base note), channel 10: 36 POTKU, 37–39 OUTO, 42 and 44 HATTU, 46 HATTU open. MIDI start and stop start and stop the groove.
  • Out: MIDI clock, start and stop over USB when CLOCK on GLO is on.

Room on the chip

The FM-1 has little flash and RAM, so suom1saundi is frugal with them:

  • Only what runs in the audio loop (voices, sequencer, effects) is compiled for speed. Everything else (generator, screen, controls, saving) is compiled for size. With the mixer, the LFOs and MAXI added, the code is still smaller than version 0.1's.
  • A step takes 7 bytes instead of 8, so a project of four patterns got smaller.
  • MAXI needs no driver of its own: the SMK-37 talks through the MIDI jack the FM-1 has anyway, and brings its own arpeggiator, chords and scales.

Building the firmware

git clone --recursive https://github.com/g0rst/suom1saundi
cd suom1saundi
sh tests/run_tests.sh        # the core's host tests
./build.sh --host            # fm1-base's simulator, then tests/run_tests.sh again
sh sim/build.sh              # the browser emulator: docs/emulator.html
./build.sh                   # the .fwsc package (needs JieLi's toolchain and the AC79 SDK)
python3 tools/manual.py      # update the manuals from the code

Where it comes from

The sequencer, controls and screen come from ro:MINImal, the 8-bit ideas from memetek-fm1, acid and filter ideas from neur0psy. The platform is fm1-base on felucca-bsp (MPL-2.0). suom1saundi itself is MIT. Not affiliated with M-VAVE.
